title: Memory Interfacing: Chips, Decoding and Chip Select
unit: Memory Interfacing, Hierarchy and Cache Mapping
quickIdea: A memory of the required size is built from smaller chips in two independent dimensions - chips side by side widen the word, rows of them extend the address range - and the high address bits are decoded into the chip-select signals that pick a row.
remember: Chips per row = required word width / chip word width. Rows (banks) = required number of words / chip word count. Total chips = rows x chips per row.
Every chip in a row receives the same low-order address bits and the same control signals; only one row's chip-select is asserted at a time.
Chip-select bits = log2(number of rows). They are the high-order bits left over after the per-chip address bits, and a decoder turns them into one-hot enables.
A chip's address range follows from which high bits its select line decodes: with select bits fixed and all other bits free, the range is (fixed bits, zeros) to (fixed bits, ones).
The decoder decides where a memory sits in the address map; with no decoder only one device could be attached, which is why the decoder is the whole of interfacing.

example.prompt: GATE CSE 2023 Q.32: a 4 KB byte-addressable memory is built from four 1 KB blocks; IA4 and IA3 go to a 2-to-4 decoder driving the chip selects, and IA11..IA0 are the 12 address lines. Give the starting address of each block.
example.work: Each block covers 1 KB, so the low 10 bits (IA9..IA0) address inside it and two further bits choose the block. Here those two bits are IA4:IA3 rather than the top two. With the ten inside bits at zero, the four select codes 00, 01, 10, 11 place IA4:IA3 = 00, 01, 10, 11, which as addresses are 0, 8, 16 and 24.
example.answer: 0, 8, 16 and 24 (option C) - not 0, 1024, 2048, 3072, which is what you get if the select bits are assumed to be the top two.

gateAngle: This question exists to punish the assumption that the chip-select bits are always the most significant ones. Read which address lines the decoder is wired to, then compute the starting addresses from those bits; the arithmetic is trivial and the reading is everything.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2023 Q.32, as worked above.
variations.why: IA4:IA3 selects the block, so consecutive blocks start 2^3 = 8 bytes apart, not 1 KB apart.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2019 Q.2: a chip-select gate decodes A15 A14 A13' A12' A11. What address range does it enable?
variations.why: The five decoded bits are fixed at 11001; the other eleven are free, so the range runs from 1100 1000 0000 0000 to 1100 1111 1111 1111.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A 64 KB x 16 memory is built from 16 KB x 8 chips with the top two address bits decoded. How many chips, how many address lines per chip, and what is the decoder?
variations.answer: Two chips per row for the 16-bit width and four rows for the 64 K words: 8 chips. Each chip takes 14 address lines, and the remaining 2 bits feed a 2-to-4 decoder that selects one row.
variations.why: It is the two-dimensional build and the decoding rule together, which is the shape the chip-count questions take.

trap.what: Assuming the chip-select bits are always the most significant address bits.
trap.why: The wiring decides, not the convention; a design may decode any bits, and the 2023 question deliberately decodes two middle bits.
trap.counterexample: In GATE CSE 2023 Q.32 the select bits are IA4:IA3, so the blocks are interleaved every 1 KB rather than laid out in 1 KB runs; answering 0, 1024, 2048, 3072 is the option (B) trap.

check.question: A system has 16 address lines and one 2 KB ROM selected when A15..A11 = 00000. What is its address range?
check.explanation: Eleven free bits below the five fixed zeros give 2^11 = 2048 locations, from all-zeros to all-ones: 0x0000 to 0x07FF.
